$comment: Per-agent Bash allowlists for the Claude Code ports of the OpenCode agents. This file owns the patterns; allow-bash.py owns the matching. Claude Code subagent frontmatter has no `permissions` field, so these cannot live in the agent files themselves. Patterns are OpenCode-style globs: * matches any run of characters, [...] is a character class passed through to the regex engine (so [^-] means 'not a dash'), everything else is literal. Matching is per command segment after splitting on ; && || | and newline.
$canonical-source: .opencode/agents/*.md is canonical -- those files are what the cloud Conductor actually executes, and OpenCode itself enforces their permission.bash block. This file is the derived port. `npm run check:bash-allowlist` fails when the two disagree in any way not listed in $divergences below. Per-pattern differences belong in that register; the three whole-file departures are described next.
$departure-1-never-beats-allow: OpenCode resolves overlapping rules by last-match-wins, which is how `git branch*: allow` followed by `git branch -*: deny` produces a denial. A pure allowlist cannot express 'allow `git switch <existing>` but refuse `git switch -c`', so allow-bash.py applies the `never` list AFTER `allow` and lets it win. The base is still default-deny: an unmatched command is refused, and `never` only exists to carve holes out of a deliberately broad allow.
$departure-2-substitution-and-redirectio: Command substitution ($(...), backticks, <(...)) and redirection to a file are refused outright for every agent, which OpenCode does not do. A prefix glob like `git log*` matches `git log > /tmp/x` and `git log; rm -rf .` -- real holes that stayed shut in OpenCode only because its `"*": ask` fallback caught them at a human prompt. A hook has no prompt to fall back on, so the holes have to be closed in the matcher. 2>&1, >&2 and >/dev/null still pass; backgrounding with a bare & is refused because it detaches the command from this gate. An external adversarial review on 27 Aug 2026 found eight bypasses of the first version of these rules and they are now closed in allow-bash.py, which additionally refuses: parent-directory traversal out of an allowlisted path, control characters, whitespace runs that split a `never` pattern, every redirection form that is not provably fd-to-fd or /dev/null, git invocations whose first argument is a flag, and the git options that hand a command line to git to execute. See the constants at the top of allow-bash.py; each carries the case that motivated it.
$departure-3-unmatched-is-deny-not-ask: OpenCode ends each bash block with `"*": ask`, so an unlisted command prompts the operator. This port refuses it instead. That is stricter, and it has a real cost: `git stash list` is read-only and harmless but appears in no OpenCode allowlist, so it is now refused rather than prompted (observed live, 27 Aug 2026). If that trade turns out wrong, allow-bash.py can emit permissionDecision 'ask' for unmatched commands while keeping `never` at 'deny' -- that would reproduce OpenCode exactly. It is a one-line change and a deliberate open question, not an oversight.
$deployment-note: This file is DATA, not the enforcement. Two things read it. (1) The project hook .claude/hooks/allow-bash.py, which Claude Code loads only in a directory whose trust dialog has been accepted. (2) The machine-scope gate ~/.claude/hooks/studio-bash-gate.py, which loads regardless of trust. Verified 27 Aug 2026 by direct experiment: in an untrusted fresh clone the write-capable predictor-builder agent loaded and executed an un-allowlisted command, because the project hook was never registered; a worktree inherits the trust of the repository it belongs to, so the exposure is specifically a NEW repository path before trust. Registering a machine-scope hook closed it: the same probe in the same untrusted clone is now refused. Therefore committing this repository's hook is necessary but NOT sufficient. Run `npm run check:bash-enforcement` to verify the machine prerequisite is installed; it fails closed and names the remediation. The machine layer is deliberately NOT in this repository, because a repository cannot be the thing that decides whether it is policed.

$filters.$purpose: Read-only output filters every agent may use, but only downstream of an allowed command -- never as the first segment. OpenCode allowed `git log | head -5` implicitly, because its prefix glob matched the whole string including the pipe. Segment-wise matching would otherwise refuse it. Restricted to commands that cannot execute their input, so `git log | sh` stays refused. Redirection to a file is blocked separately, which is what keeps awk/sed from writing.

$unmatched.$comment: Capability-aware policy for a command that matches no allow pattern. Write-capable roles are refused: an autonomous or headless agent has nobody to prompt, so 'ask' would be an unattended refusal at best. Read-only roles are referred to the operator instead, which recovers OpenCode's `"*": ask` behaviour exactly where it is safe -- the worst case is approving an unanticipated read such as `git stash list`. Ceiling and `never` refusals are never downgraded to a prompt.

$neverForAnyAgent.$comment: A floor applied to every role before the $unmatched decision, mirroring the machine ceiling. Without it a read-only role's empty `never` list let a mutation fall through to the read-only ASK path: predictor-critic running `git commit -m x` was referred to the operator instead of refused. A prompt is not an acceptable answer to a mutation from a role that is defined as unable to mutate.

predictor-conductor.$purpose: Read-only orientation plus the two tracked review bridges. Never runs gates itself.

predictor-builder.$purpose: Sole write-capable role. Git writes must route through the owner-* wrappers, which consult config/pre-live-owner-authority.json. The `never` list is what makes that binding rather than advisory.
predictor-builder.$divergence-1: OpenCode denies `git branch -*`, which -- under its last-match-wins ordering -- also refuses read-only queries like `git branch --show-current`. That is an over-broad deny, not a decision. Here `git branch` is allowlisted by its read-only forms instead, so querying works and creation/deletion/rename stay refused by default.
predictor-builder.$divergence-2: OpenCode allows `git checkout*` with only `-b`/`-B` denied, which leaves `git checkout HEAD -- src/` allowed. That discards uncommitted work in the tree the builder is supposed to be protecting. Navigation is now allowlisted as `git switch|checkout [^-]*` (a non-flag first argument) and the pathspec form is denied outright.

predictor-critic.$purpose: Read-only inspection only. Deliberately cannot run tests or builds; that evidence belongs to predictor-release-verifier.

predictor-visual-qa.$purpose: Browser/journey evidence. Playwright lanes only, no general gate set.

predictor-release-verifier.$purpose: Read-only gate and CI evidence. Same git reads as the critic, plus the authoritative gate set.

$layering: machine ceiling (~/.claude/hooks/studio-bash-ceiling.json) -> repository allowlist (this file) -> effective policy. A repository may narrow what its agents run; it can never widen past the ceiling and can never switch the gate off. The machine gate reads this file as JSON data and never imports or executes anything from the repository, so a hostile clone cannot run code at machine scope. Verified against a repository that granted itself allow:[*]: mutation, publication, privilege change, network fetch-to-shell and secret-path reads all remained refused.
